ry disease difficult ckd complications. kdigo also recommends using the kidney failure risk equation (kfre) in ckd g3–g5. a 5-year kidney-failure risk around 3–5% may help guide nephrology referral; >10% risk over 2 years can prompt multidisciplinary care, while >40% over 2 years can guide krt preparation. (kdigo) 18. prepare for kidney replacement therapy do not wait until the patient crashes. discuss: hemodialysis peritoneal dialysis kidney transplant conservative kidney management where appropriate. kdigo suggests beginning dialysis-access/transplant preparation when: egfr \u003c15–20 ml/min/1.73 m² or estimated 2-year krt risk >40%. (kdigo) for hemodialysis, plan an av fistula in advance when appropriate rather than repeatedly using temporary central venous catheters. 19. when do you start dialysis? this is extremely important: do not start dialysis simply because creatinine is high. and do not say: “egfr \u003c15 automatically means dialysis.” kdigo says dialysis initiation should be based on a composite of: symptoms + signs + laboratory abnormalities + gfr + quality of life + patient preferences. it commonly, but not always, becomes necessary around: egfr 5–10 ml/min/1.73 m². (kdigo) for exams, remember aeiou: a — acidosis severe metabolic acidosis refractory to medical therapy. e — electrolytes especially refractory/severe hyperkalemia. i — intoxications dialyzable toxins where relevant. o — overload pulmonary edema/fluid overload refractory to diuretics. u — uremia such as: uremic encephalopathy uremic pericarditis severe refractory nausea/vomiting severe symptomatic uremia bleeding related to uremia refractory pruritus in appropriate context. 20. monitoring at follow-up monitor: bp + weight + edema/volume status + urine output + creatinine/egfr + urine acr + k⁺ + na⁺ + hco₃⁻ + hb + ca²⁺ + phosphate ± pth + glucose/hba1c. the frequency depends on ckd stage and progression risk. a falling egfr, rapidly increasing albuminuria, recurrent complications or g4/g5 disease means closer follow-up. the ward-round answer to memorize if your consultant asks: “how will you manage this ckd patient?” your sequence should be: first, assess the patient clinically, determine the cause of ckd and classify the disease according to egfr and albuminuria. i will then treat the underlying cause and slow progression by controlling blood pressure and diabetes, reducing sodium intake to \u003c2 g/day, maintaining protein at approximately 0.8 g/kg/day in non-dialysis g3–g5 ckd, individualizing fluid intake, encouraging exercise, smoking cessation, avoiding nephrotoxins, treating albuminuria with acei/arb and using sglt2 inhibitors where indicated. second, i will screen for and treat ckd complications including fluid overload, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia, ckd-mineral bone disorder, cardiovascular disease and uremic manifestations. finally, in advanced progressive ckd i will involve nephrology early, provide education regarding kidney replacement therapy, prepare appropriate dialysis access or transplant evaluation, and initiate dialysis based on symptoms and complications rather than egfr alone. numbers you should not forget na \u003c2 g/day = salt \u003c5 g/day protein = 0.8 g/kg/day in g3–g5 non-dialysis ckd exercise ≥150 min/week sbp \u003c120 mmhg when tolerated using standardized measurement sglt2i generally from egfr ≥20 when indicated metabolic acidosis: consider active correction especially hco₃⁻ \u003c18 mmol/l plan krt around egfr \u003c15–20 or high predicted kidney-failure risk dialysis = clinical indications, commonly around egfr 5–10, not creatinine alone. (kdigo) ulichosema kina msingi mzuri, lakini kuna corrections chache muhimu. kwa ckd, usikariri kwamba kila mgonjwa lazima anywe 1.5 l au 2 l, na pia “2 g sodium” si sawa na “2 g salt.” ckd management — framework rahisi kwa practical purposes unaweza kuigawa: 1. slow/control ckd progression → lifestyle + control underlying disease + renoprotective drugs. 2. prevent and treat complications → anemia, hyperkalemia, acidosis, ckd-mbd, fluid overload, cvd, etc. 3. advanced kidney failure care → education/preparation for kidney replacement therapy, dialysis/transplant when indicated. kwa sehemu unayojifunza sasa — slowing progression: 1. sodium restriction kdigo recommends: sodium \u003c2 g/day = sodium chloride (salt) \u003c5 g/day. (kdigo) kwa nini? nacl ina: na = 23 cl = 35.5 total = 58.5 kwa hiyo sodium ni approximately 39% ya uzito wa salt. so: 5 g nacl × 0.39 ≈ 2 g sodium. kwa mgonjwa unaweza kusema: “chumvi yote unayotumia kwa siku iwe chini ya gramu 5, yaani karibu chini kidogo ya kijiko kimoja cha chai, na hii ni pamoja na chumvi iliyopo tayari kwenye chakula.” siyo kumpa 5 g table salt halafu bado ale processed foods. total sodium from everything counts. faida: ↓ sodium → ↓ fluid retention → ↓ bp → ↓ proteinuria/intraglomerular stress → slower ckd progression. 2. protein kwa adult ckd g3–g5 ambaye hayuko dialysis: protein ≈ 0.8 g/kg/day. kdigo pia inapendekeza kuepuka high-protein intake >1.3 g/kg/day kwa walio katika risk ya progression. (kdigo) example: patient 70 kg: 0.8 × 70 = 56 g protein/day. concept yako ilikuwa sahihi: excessive protein inaweza kuongeza intraglomerular pressure/hyperfiltration, hivyo inaweza kuchangia progression. lakini usifanye severe protein restriction bila indication, kwa sababu unaweza kusababisha protein-energy wasting/malnutrition. (kdigo) kwa dialysis, protein requirement huwa higher, si 0.8 g/kg/day; commonly around 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day depending on modality/nutritional status. (kdigo) 3. water/fluid — hapa correction kubwa usiseme: “every ckd patient should drink plenty of water.” na pia usikariri: “every ckd patient gets 1.5 l/day.” fluid prescription ni individualized. patient ambaye: ana adequate urine output, hana edema, hana heart failure, hana hyponatremia, usually hahitaji routine severe fluid restriction; drink according to thirst/clinical need. lakini ukiwa na: oliguria/anuria generalized edema pulmonary edema heart failure hyponatremia advanced ckd with volume overload → fluid restriction may be necessary. kwa oliguric/advanced patients, practical prescriptions are often based on previous 24-hour urine output + allowance for insensible losses, rather than blindly giving everybody 1 l or 1.5 l. kwa hiyo ward round ukisema: “fluid intake will be individualized according to urine output, volume status, serum sodium and presence of edema or heart failure.” hiyo ni stronger answer kuliko kusema “2 l/day.” kdigo also emphasizes individualized advice in advanced ckd and in patients at risk of fluid retention. (kdigo) 4. exercise siyo lazima exactly 30 minutes every day. kdigo target ni approximately: ≥150 minutes/week of moderate-intensity physical activity, adjusted to cardiovascular and physical tolerance. (kdigo) unaweza kugawa: 30 min × 5 days/week = 150 min/week. also reduce sedentary behavior. 5. healthy diet / fibre correct. encourage predominantly healthy foods: vegetables + fruits + whole grains + legumes + fibre + plant-based proteins + unsaturated fats, while reducing processed meats, refined carbohydrates and sugary drinks. (kdigo) lakini important caveat: usiseme kila ckd patient ale unlimited fruits/vegetables. kama ana hyperkalemia, potassium intake needs individualized modification; kdigo recommends focusing particularly on highly bioavailable potassium from processed foods when hyperkalemia is present/risk is high. (kdigo) 6. co"},{"id":"pdf-0","disease":"Acute decompensated heart failure","label":"ADHF series","origin":"ADHF Series.pdf","type":"pdf","pages":9,"illustrations":2,"tables":7,"sections":[{"name":"ADHF series","html":"\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 1\u003c/div>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 1\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 1\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>ACUTE DECOMPENSATED HEART FAILURE\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>(ADHF)\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ADHF Series\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) is: Rapid onset or worsening of signs and symptoms\u003cbr>of heart failure require urgent evaluation and treatment, usually leading to hospitalization.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It may occur in: Known chronic HF patient with worsening OR New-onset heart failure\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Main pathophysiology:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Congestion (wet”) → elevated filling pressures   2. Hypoperfusion (“cold”) → reduced cardiac output\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">COMMON PRECIPITATING FACTORS\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">“CHAMPIT”\u003c/h3>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Cause\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Explanation\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>C\u003c/td>\u003ctd>ACS / ischemia\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>H\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hypertensive emergency\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 2\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>A\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Arrhythmias (AFib common)\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>M\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Mechanical causes (MR, VSD, tamponade)\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>P\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Pulmonary embolism\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>I\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Infection\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>T\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Treatment noncompliance\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Other causes:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  CKD/AKI   •  Excess salt/fluid intake   •  Anemia   •  Thyroid disease   •  Drugs:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o NSAIDs   o Steroids   o Verapamil/diltiazem   o TZDs\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. When you see a patient with Acute Decompensated Heart Failure\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">First ask yourself:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Is the patient wet or dry?  Is the patient warm or cold?\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">HEMODYNAMIC CLASSIFICATION\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Warm/Wet – Cold/Wet – Warm/Dry – Cold/Dry\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This classification guides management.\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Profile\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Perfusion\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Congestion\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Meaning\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Warm &amp; Dry\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Adequate\u003c/td>\u003ctd>No\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Compensated\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Warm &amp; Wet\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Adequate\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Yes\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Most common ADHF\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Cold &amp; Wet\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Poor\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Yes\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Cardiogenic shock phenotype\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Cold &amp; Dry\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Poor\u003c/td>\u003ctd>No\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Severe low output\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This gives the phenotype and treatment direction. Your uploaded notes also use this same  wet/cold framework.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Check if the patient is “WET”\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 3\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Wet means congested / volume overloaded / high LV filling pressure.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Look for:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Symptoms\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Signs\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Labs/Imaging\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Dyspnea\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Raised JVP\u003c/td>\u003ctd>High BNP/NT-proBNP\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Orthopnea\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Crackles\u003c/td>\u003ctd>CXR pulmonary edema\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>PND\u003c/td>\u003ctd>S3 gallop\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Dilated IVC\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Leg swelling\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Peripheral edema\u003c/td>\u003ctd>B-lines on lung US\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Weight gain\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hepatomegaly/ascites\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If wet → the main drug is IV loop diuretic.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Check if the patient is “COLD”\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Cold means low cardiac output / poor perfusion.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Look for:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Symptoms\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Signs\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Labs\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Fatigue\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Cold extremities\u003c/td>\u003ctd>High lactate\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Confusion\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Narrow pulse pressure\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Worsening creatinine\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Dizziness\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Poor capillary refill\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Metabolic acidosis\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Reduced urine\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hypotension\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If cold → think inotrope ± vasopressor.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Classify the phenotype\u003c/h3>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Phenotype\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Meaning\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Example\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Warm + Wet\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Congested but perfusing\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Most common ADHF\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Cold + Wet\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Congested + hypoperfused\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Dangerous, may be shock\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Cold + Dry\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hypoperfused, not congested\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Low output/underfilled\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Warm + Dry\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Stable/compensated\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Optimize chronic treatment\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">5. If Warm + Wet\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is the commonest ADHF pattern.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 4\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Management\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">For diuresis  Give:\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 4\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 4\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Furosemide 20–40 mg IV stat if diuretic-naïve.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If already on oral loop diuretic:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Give 1–2 times the home dose as IV equivalent.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Example:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Oral furosemide 80 mg/day ≈ IV furosemide 40 mg/day.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Maintenance\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Furosemide IV BD/TDS depending response  OR   •  Infusion 5–20 mg/hour\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Add vasodilator if BP allows\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If SBP &gt;100–110 mmHg and pulmonary edema/hypertension:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Nitroglycerin IV 5–10 mcg/min, titrate every 5–10 minutes.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Monitor\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Urine output   •  Daily weight   •  BP   •  Creatinine   •  K⁺, Mg²⁺   •  Symptoms\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">6. If Cold + Wet\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is dangerous because the patient has both congestion and low perfusion.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If SBP &gt;90 mmHg\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">For congestion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Furosemide IV carefully\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">For low output\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 5\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Dobutamine 2–20 mcg/kg/min IV infusion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If BP allows\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Consider vasodilator cautiously.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If SBP &lt;90 mmHg or shock\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">First support BP\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Norepinephrine 0.01–1 mcg/kg/min IV infusion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Then support contractility\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Add dobutamine 2–20 mcg/kg/min if low cardiac output persists.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Then remove fluid\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Diuretics once perfusion is supported.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">7. If Cold + Dry\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ask: is the patient underfilled?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If yes:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Normal saline 250 mL bolus, then reassess.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If still cold:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Dobutamine 2–20 mcg/kg/min  OR   •  Milrinone 0.125–0.75 mcg/kg/min\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Avoid aggressive diuresis here.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">8. If Warm + Dry\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patient is compensated.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Now focus on chronic HFrEF mortality-reducing drugs:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. ARNI/ACEI/ARB   2. Beta blocker   3. MRA   4. SGLT2 inhibitor\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 6\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These are core guideline-directed therapies for HFrEF; ESC also recommends SGLT2 inhibitors\u003cbr>for HFmrEF/HFpEF to reduce HF hospitalization or cardiovascular death.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">9. Medication series\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">A. Furosemide\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use: wet ADHF.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Dose\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Start: 20–40 mg IV stat   •  Repeat/escalate if poor response   •  Infusion: 5–20 mg/hour\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Loading?\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">No formal loading dose.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Maintenance\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">IV BD/TDS or infusion.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia, dehydration.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Serious adverse effects\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">AKI, severe hypotension, arrhythmia, ototoxicity.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">B. Metolazone\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use: diuretic resistance.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Dose\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  2.5–5 mg PO, 30–60 minutes before loop diuretic.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Severe hypokalemia, hyponatremia, dehydration, AKI.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">C. Nitroglycerin\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use: wet ADHF with high BP/pulmonary edema.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 7\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Dose\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Start 5–10 mcg/min IV   •  Titrate upward every 5–10 minutes   •  Usual 20–200 mcg/min\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Headache, flushing, hypotension.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Avoid\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">SBP &lt;90, RV infarction, severe aortic stenosis, recent sildenafil/tadalafil.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">D. Dobutamine\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use: cold ADHF / cardiogenic shock.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Dose\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  2–20 mcg/kg/min IV infusion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Tachycardia, arrhythmia, ischemia.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">E. Norepinephrine\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use: cardiogenic shock with hypotension.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Dose\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  0.01–1 mcg/kg/min IV infusion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Arrhythmia, peripheral ischemia, severe hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">F. Sacubitril/Valsartan\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use: stable HFrEF, not acute shock.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Dose\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Start 24/26 mg BID if low BP/renal impairment/ACEI-naïve   •  Start 49/51 mg BID if previously tolerating ACEI/ARB\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 8\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Target 97/103 mg BID\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Important\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Need 36-hour washout after ACE inhibitor.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypotension, hyperkalemia, AKI, angioedema.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">G. symptoms of heart failure require urgent evaluation and treatment, usually leading to hospitalization. it may occur in: known chronic hf patient with worsening or new-onset heart failure main pathophysiology: 1. congestion (wet”) → elevated filling pressures 2. hypoperfusion (“cold”) → reduced cardiac output common precipitating factors “champit” cause explanation c acs / ischemia h hypertensive emergency a arrhythmias (afib common) m mechanical causes (mr, vsd, tamponade) p pulmonary embolism i infection t treatment noncompliance other causes: • ckd/aki • excess salt/fluid intake • anemia • thyroid disease • drugs: o nsaids o steroids o verapamil/diltiazem o tzds 1. when you see a patient with acute decompensated heart failure first ask yourself: is the patient wet or dry? is the patient warm or cold? hemodynamic classification warm/wet – cold/wet – warm/dry – cold/dry this classification guides management. profile perfusion congestion meaning warm & dry adequate no compensated warm & wet adequate yes most common adhf cold & wet poor yes cardiogenic shock phenotype cold & dry poor no severe low output this gives the phenotype and treatment direction. your uploaded notes also use this same wet/cold framework. 2. check if the patient is “wet” wet means congested / volume overloaded / high lv filling pressure. look for: symptoms signs labs/imaging dyspnea raised jvp high bnp/nt-probnp orthopnea crackles cxr pulmonary edema pnd s3 gallop dilated ivc leg swelling peripheral edema b-lines on lung us weight gain hepatomegaly/ascites if wet → the main drug is iv loop diuretic. 3. check if the patient is “cold” cold means low cardiac output / poor perfusion. look for: symptoms signs labs fatigue cold extremities high lactate confusion narrow pulse pressure worsening creatinine dizziness poor capillary refill metabolic acidosis reduced urine hypotension if cold → think inotrope ± vasopressor. 4. classify the phenotype phenotype meaning example warm + wet congested but perfusing most common adhf cold + wet congested + hypoperfused dangerous, may be shock cold + dry hypoperfused, not congested low output/underfilled warm + dry stable/compensated optimize chronic treatment 5. if warm + wet this is the commonest adhf pattern. management for diuresis give: furosemide 20–40 mg iv stat if diuretic-naïve. if already on oral loop diuretic: give 1–2 times the home dose as iv equivalent. example: oral furosemide 80 mg/day ≈ iv furosemide 40 mg/day. maintenance • furosemide iv bd/tds depending response or • infusion 5–20 mg/hour add vasodilator if bp allows if sbp >100–110 mmhg and pulmonary edema/hypertension: nitroglycerin iv 5–10 mcg/min, titrate every 5–10 minutes. monitor • urine output • daily weight • bp • creatinine • k⁺, mg²⁺ • symptoms 6. if cold + wet this is dangerous because the patient has both congestion and low perfusion. if sbp >90 mmhg for congestion • furosemide iv carefully for low output • dobutamine 2–20 mcg/kg/min iv infusion if bp allows • consider vasodilator cautiously. if sbp \u003c90 mmhg or shock first support bp • norepinephrine 0.01–1 mcg/kg/min iv infusion then support contractility • add dobutamine 2–20 mcg/kg/min if low cardiac output persists. then remove fluid • diuretics once perfusion is supported. 7. if cold + dry ask: is the patient underfilled? if yes: normal saline 250 ml bolus, then reassess. if still cold: • dobutamine 2–20 mcg/kg/min or • milrinone 0.125–0.75 mcg/kg/min avoid aggressive diuresis here. 8. if warm + dry patient is compensated. now focus on chronic hfref mortality-reducing drugs: 1. arni/acei/arb 2. beta blocker 3. mra 4. sglt2 inhibitor these are core guideline-directed therapies for hfref; esc also recommends sglt2 inhibitors for hfmref/hfpef to reduce hf hospitalization or cardiovascular death. 9. medication series a. furosemide use: wet adhf. dose • start: 20–40 mg iv stat • repeat/escalate if poor response • infusion: 5–20 mg/hour loading? no formal loading dose. maintenance iv bd/tds or infusion. side effects hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia, dehydration. serious adverse effects aki, severe hypotension, arrhythmia, ototoxicity. b. metolazone use: diuretic resistance. dose • 2.5–5 mg po, 30–60 minutes before loop diuretic. side effects severe hypokalemia, hyponatremia, dehydration, aki. c. nitroglycerin use: wet adhf with high bp/pulmonary edema. dose • start 5–10 mcg/min iv • titrate upward every 5–10 minutes • usual 20–200 mcg/min side effects headache, flushing, hypotension. avoid sbp \u003c90, rv 1\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE (CKD)\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Definition\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive and irreversible loss of kidney function\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">characterized by abnormalities in kidney structure or function that persist for at least three\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">months and have implications for health. According to the KDIGO guidelines, CKD is diagnosed\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">when there is either a reduction in the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) to less than 60\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">mL/min/1.73 m² for more than three months or evidence of kidney damage regardless of GFR.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Evidence of kidney damage may include albuminuria, abnormalities in urine sediment,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">electrolyte disturbances due to tubular disorders, structural abnormalities detected by imaging, or\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">histological abnormalities on kidney biopsy. CKD is an important global health problem because\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">it increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, hospitalization, kidney failure, and premature\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">death.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">MUST KNOW\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">KDIGO Criteria for CKD\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 2\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD is present if either of the following persists for ≥3 months:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. GFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73m²\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Evidence of kidney damage:\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Albuminuria (ACR ≥30 mg/g)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Urine sediment abnormalities\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Electrolyte abnormalities due to tubular disorders\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Histological abnormalities\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Structural abnormalities on imaging\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o History of kidney transplantation\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">NORMAL KIDNEY PHYSIOLOGY\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Before understanding CKD, one must first understand how the kidneys normally function. The\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">kidneys are paired retroperitoneal organs responsible for maintaining the internal environment of\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">the body. They regulate water balance, electrolyte concentrations, acid-base status, blood\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">pressure, erythropoiesis, and bone metabolism. Each kidney contains approximately one million\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">nephrons, which are the functional units responsible for filtering blood and forming urine. A\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">nephron consists of the glomerulus, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">tubule, and collecting duct.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The glomerulus acts as a highly specialized filtration barrier. Blood enters through the afferent\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">arteriole and leaves via the efferent arteriole. Filtration occurs across three layers: the fenestrated\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane, and podocytes. Water and small solutes pass\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">through this barrier into Bowman&#x27;s capsule, while large proteins and blood cells are retained\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">within the circulation. The amount of filtrate formed per minute is called the glomerular filtration\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">rate (GFR), which normally ranges from approximately 90–120 mL/min/1.73 m² in healthy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">adults.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">After filtration, the renal tubules modify the filtrate extensively. The proximal tubule reabsorbs\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">nearly all glucose, amino acids, and most sodium and bicarbonate. The loop of Henle establishes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">the concentration gradient necessary for urine concentration. The distal convoluted tubule and\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 3\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">collecting duct are regulated by hormones such as aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone (ADH),\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">allowing fine adjustment of sodium and water balance.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In addition to filtration and excretion, the kidneys perform important endocrine functions.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Specialized interstitial cells produce erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates red blood cell\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">production in the bone marrow. The kidneys also convert inactive vitamin D into its active form,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), which is essential for calcium absorption and bone health.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Furthermore, the kidneys participate in blood pressure regulation through the renin-angiotensin-\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">aldosterone system (RAAS). Any chronic injury to the kidneys disrupts these functions and leads\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">to the diverse manifestations observed in CKD.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">MUST KNOW\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Major functions of the kidney\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Excretion of waste products\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Urea\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Creatinine\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Uric acid\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Drugs and toxins\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Regulation of:\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Water balance\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Sodium\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Potassium\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Calcium\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Phosphate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Acid-base balance\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Endocrine functions:\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Erythropoietin production\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Vitamin D activation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Renin secretion\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 4\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">ETIOLOGY OF CKD\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Chronic kidney disease is not a single disease but rather a syndrome resulting from many\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">different disorders that cause progressive nephron destruction. The prevalence of specific causes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">varies by region. In developed countries, diabetes mellitus and hypertension account for the\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">majority of cases. In sub-Saharan Africa, however, hypertension, chronic glomerulonephritis,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">HIV-associated nephropathy, and obstructive uropathy remain major contributors.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Diabetes Mellitus\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Diabetes mellitus is currently the leading cause of CKD worldwide. Chronic hyperglycemia\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">causes glycation of proteins within the glomerular basement membrane and mesangium. This\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">results in thickening of the basement membrane, mesangial expansion, podocyte injury, and\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">glomerulosclerosis. Initially, diabetic patients develop hyperfiltration and microalbuminuria.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Over time, persistent proteinuria and fibrosis lead to progressive decline in renal function.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertension\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertension damages the small arteries and arterioles supplying the kidneys. Persistent high\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">pressure causes hyaline arteriosclerosis, narrowing of blood vessels, and ischemic injury to\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">nephrons. The glomeruli gradually become sclerotic, and the kidneys shrink in size.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertension is both a cause and a consequence of CKD, creating a vicious cycle that accelerates\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">disease progression.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Chronic Glomerulonephritis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Glomerulonephritis encompasses a group of immune-mediated diseases affecting the glomeruli.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Persistent inflammation results in glomerular destruction and fibrosis. Patients may initially\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">present with hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, or nephrotic syndrome before progressing to\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CKD.\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Obstructive Uropathy\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 5\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Long-standing obstruction of urine flow, such as from benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH),\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">prostate cancer, ureteric stones, or strictures, causes back pressure on the kidneys. Persistent\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">obstruction leads to hydronephrosis, tubular atrophy, and irreversible nephron loss.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">HIV-associated Nephropathy (HIVAN)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">HIV can directly infect renal epithelial cells, leading to collapsing focal segmental\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). Patients often present with nephrotic-range proteinuria and rapidly\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">progressive renal failure. Unlike many other causes of CKD, HIVAN often produces enlarged\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">kidneys on ultrasound.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Pathophysiology\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The progression of chronic kidney disease is not simply a consequence of the initial kidney\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">injury but is largely driven by maladaptive responses that occur in the remaining functioning\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">nephrons. When a significant number of nephrons are lost, the surviving nephrons undergo\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">compensatory hypertrophy and hyperfiltration in an attempt to maintain overall kidney function.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Initially, this adaptation is beneficial because it preserves GFR and delays the onset of\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">symptoms. However, the increased intraglomerular pressure generated by hyperfiltration\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">gradually damages the glomerular capillary wall. This leads to proteinuria, activation of\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">inflammatory pathways, oxidative stress, and the release of profibrotic cytokines such as\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β).\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Over time, the persistent inflammatory process results in mesangial expansion,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">glomerulosclerosis, and tubulointerstitial fibrosis. Fibrosis progressively replaces functional\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">renal tissue, leading to further nephron loss. As the number of functioning nephrons declines, the\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">kidneys lose their ability to regulate fluid balance, electrolyte homeostasis, acid-base balance,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">erythropoietin production, and vitamin D metabolism. Consequently, patients develop\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">complications such as edema, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia, secondary\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">hyperparathyroidism, and uremia. This self-perpetuating cycle of nephron loss and fibrosis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">eventually culminates in end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), at which point renal replacement\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">therapy becomes necessary\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 6\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Diagnosis of Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The diagnosis of CKD is based on two fundamental criteria:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Evidence of kidney damage, OR   2. Reduced kidney function (eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73m²)\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">AND\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These abnormalities must persist for at least 3 months.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Clinical Evaluation\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The diagnosis starts with a careful history and physical examination.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">History\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ask about:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Duration of symptoms (&gt;3 months suggests CKD)\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Hypertension\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Diabetes mellitus\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Recurrent urinary tract infections\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Hematuria\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Frothy urine (proteinuria)\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Reduced urine output\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Nocturia\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Facial puffiness or leg swelling\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>History of kidney stones\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Use of nephrotoxic drugs\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o NSAIDs   o Herbal medicines   o Aminoglycosides   •  Family history\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Polycystic kidney disease   o CKD   •  Autoimmune diseases\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o SLE   o Vasculitis\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Physical Examination\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Look for:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">General\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 7\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Pallor → anemia   •  Scratch marks → uremic pruritus   •  Muscle wasting   •  Weight loss\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Vital signs\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hypertension (very common)   •  Tachypnea if acidosis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Fluid overload\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Raised JVP   •  Bilateral pitting edema   •  Pulmonary edema   •  Ascites\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Bone disease\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Bone tenderness   •  Skeletal deformities\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Neurological\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Confusion   •  Peripheral neuropathy   •  Asterixis (advanced uremia)\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Laboratory Diagnosis\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">A. Serum Creatinine\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Serum creatinine is the most commonly used marker of kidney function.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A raised creatinine suggests reduced GFR.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">However, creatinine alone does not diagnose CKD because:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>It varies with muscle mass\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>It may be elevated in AKI\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Elderly patients may have normal creatinine despite reduced GFR\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Therefore:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 8\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Always calculate eGFR.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">B. Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">eGFR is the best routine measure of kidney function.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It is calculated from:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Serum creatinine   •  Age   •  Sex   •  Race\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD is diagnosed if:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73m²\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">for ≥ 3 months\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">OR\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Evidence of kidney damage\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">despite normal eGFR.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD Staging (KDIGO)\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Stage\u003c/td>\u003ctd>eGFR (mL/min/1.73m²)\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Description\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>G1\u003c/td>\u003ctd>≥90\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Normal/high\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>G2\u003c/td>\u003ctd>60–89\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Mild reduction\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>G3a\u003c/td>\u003ctd>45–59\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Mild-moderate\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>G3b\u003c/td>\u003ctd>30–44\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Moderate-severe\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>G4\u003c/td>\u003ctd>15–29\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Severe\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>G5\u003c/td>\u003ctd>&lt;15\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Kidney failure\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">C. Urinalysis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Urinalysis is one of the most important investigations.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Look for:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Proteinuria\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Suggests:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 9\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Diabetic nephropathy   •  Glomerulonephritis   •  FSGS   •  HIVAN\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Hematuria\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Suggests:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Glomerulonephritis   •  Lupus nephritis   •  Vasculitis   •  Stones\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">RBC casts\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Strongly suggest:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Glomerulonephritis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">WBC casts\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Suggest:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Interstitial nephritis   •  Pyelonephritis\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">D. Albuminuria\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Measure:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Urine Albumin Creatinine Ratio (ACR)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Persistent albuminuria is an early marker of CKD.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">KDIGO Albuminuria Classification\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Category\u003c/td>\u003ctd>ACR\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>A1\u003c/td>\u003ctd>&lt;30 mg/g\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>A2\u003c/td>\u003ctd>30–300 mg/g\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>A3\u003c/td>\u003ctd>&gt;300 mg/g\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">E. Electrolytes\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Check:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 10\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Potassium\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hyperkalemia occurs because the kidneys cannot excrete potassium.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Bicarbonate\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Low bicarbonate indicates:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Metabolic acidosis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Calcium and Phosphate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD typically causes:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  ↓ Calcium   •  ↑ Phosphate\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Usually elevated.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why is PTH elevated?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">As kidney function declines:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Phosphate excretion decreases\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Serum phosphate rises\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Calcium falls\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Vitamin D activation decreases\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">5. Intestinal calcium absorption falls\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">6. Hypocalcemia stimulates parathyroid glands\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 11\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">7. Secondary hyperparathyroidism develops.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Imaging\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ultrasound KUB (Kidney-Ureter-Bladder)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ultrasound is the imaging investigation of choice.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Typical CKD findings\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Small kidneys   •  Shrunken cortex   •  Increased cortical echogenicity   •  Poor corticomedullary differentiation\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Viva Question\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Which CKD conditions produce enlarged kidneys?\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Answer\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Diabetic nephropathy\u003cbr>2. HIV-associated nephropathy\u003cbr>3. Amyloidosis\u003cbr>4. Polycystic kidney disease\u003cbr>5. Multiple myeloma\u003cbr>6. Acute interstitial nephritis\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Kidney Biopsy\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Kidney biopsy is not required in every patient.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It is indicated when the cause is unclear or when a specific diagnosis will alter management.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Indications\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Nephrotic syndrome\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Rapidly progressive renal failure\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Unexplained proteinuria\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Persistent hematuria\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Suspected lupus nephritis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Suspected vasculitis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Diagnostic Criteria of CKD (KDIGO)\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 12\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A patient has CKD if one or both of the following are present for ≥3 months:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Reduced kidney function\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">eGFR\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">&lt;60 mL/min/1.73m²\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">OR\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Evidence of kidney damage\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examples:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Albuminuria (ACR ≥30 mg/g)\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Urine sediment abnormalities\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Electrolyte abnormalities due to tubular disorders\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Histological abnormalities\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Structural abnormalities on imaging\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>History of kidney transplantation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Differentiating CKD from AKI\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is a very common viva question.\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Feature\u003c/td>\u003ctd>CKD\u003c/td>\u003ctd>AKI\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Duration\u003c/td>\u003ctd>&gt;3 months\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hours to weeks\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Kidney size\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Small\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Normal/enlarged\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Anemia\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Common\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Uncommon\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Hypocalcemia\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Common\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Rare\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Hyperphosphatemia\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Common\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Less common\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Osteodystrophy\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Present\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Absent\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Previous creatinine\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Elevated for months\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Recently elevated\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Symptoms\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Chronic\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Acute\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE (CKD)\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">SECTION: MANAGEMENT OF CKD (MMED / Davidson / KDIGO Style)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD management is not simply about lowering creatinine or delaying dialysis. It is a\u003cbr>comprehensive strategy aimed at slowing disease progression, preventing cardiovascular\u003cbr>complications, treating metabolic abnormalities, improving quality of life, and preparing\u003cbr>patients for renal replacement therapy when necessary. Management depends on the stage of\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 13\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD, the underlying cause, and the presence of complications such as anemia, hyperkalemia,\u003cbr>metabolic acidosis, or CKD-mineral bone disease.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The first principle in CKD management is to identify and treat the underlying cause. A patient\u003cbr>with diabetic nephropathy requires aggressive glycemic control, whereas a patient with lupus\u003cbr>nephritis may require immunosuppressive therapy. Similarly, obstructive uropathy should be\u003cbr>relieved promptly to prevent further nephron loss. Once the cause is identified, attention is\u003cbr>directed toward slowing progression of CKD and managing its complications.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. GENERAL MEASURES\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">All patients with CKD should receive counseling regarding lifestyle modifications. Salt intake\u003cbr>should be restricted to less than 2 g of sodium per day because excessive sodium promotes fluid\u003cbr>retention, hypertension, and proteinuria. Smoking cessation is strongly recommended because\u003cbr>smoking accelerates decline in kidney function and increases cardiovascular risk. Patients should\u003cbr>maintain a healthy body weight and engage in regular physical activity if tolerated. Nephrotoxic\u003cbr>drugs, especially NSAIDs, should be avoided because they reduce renal blood flow and may\u003cbr>precipitate AKI on top of CKD.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients should also receive vaccination against influenza, pneumococcus, hepatitis B, and\u003cbr>COVID-19 when appropriate because infections contribute significantly to morbidity and\u003cbr>mortality in CKD.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypertension is both a cause and a consequence of CKD. Poorly controlled blood pressure\u003cbr>accelerates nephron loss and increases the risk of cardiovascular events.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to KDIGO and AHA guidelines:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Target BP\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>&lt;130/80 mmHg in most patients with CKD.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>In patients with significant proteinuria, even stricter control may be beneficial if\u003cbr>tolerated.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ACE Inhibitors and ARBs\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ACE inhibitors and ARBs are the preferred antihypertensive agents, especially in patients with\u003cbr>proteinuria. These drugs reduce intraglomerular pressure by dilating the efferent arteriole,\u003cbr>thereby reducing proteinuria and slowing progression of CKD.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ACE inhibitors\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examples:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 14\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Enalapril   •  Lisinopril   •  Ramipril\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Enalapril dose\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Start:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  2.5–5 mg once daily\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Increase gradually to:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  10–20 mg daily   •  Maximum: 40 mg/day\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ARBs\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examples:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Losartan   •  Valsartan   •  Telmisartan\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Losartan dose\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Start:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  25–50 mg OD\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Target:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  100 mg OD\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side Effects of ACE inhibitors\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Most examiners ask this.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Common side effects include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Dry cough   •  Hyperkalemia   •  Hypotension   •  Dizziness   •  Angioedema   •  Increase in creatinine\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 15\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side Effects of ARBs\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hyperkalemia   •  Hypotension   •  Worsening renal function\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Importantly:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ARBs do not usually cause cough.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Caution\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ACE inhibitors and ARBs should be used cautiously in:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Bilateral renal artery stenosis   •  Severe hyperkalemia   •  AKI   •  Symptomatic hypotension\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">When should ACEi or ARB be stopped\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Temporarily stop if:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Creatinine rises &gt;30% from baseline.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Potassium &gt;5.5–6 mmol/L.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Severe dehydration.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Acute illness causing AKI.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. DIABETES MANAGEMENT\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Diabetes is the commonest cause of CKD worldwide. Strict glycemic control slows progression\u003cbr>of nephropathy and reduces cardiovascular complications.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Metformin\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Metformin is often first-line therapy in type 2 diabetes.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">However:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use according to eGFR\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">eGFR Recommendation  &gt;45  Continue  30–45 Reduce dose  &lt;30  STOP\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 16\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why stop metformin?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Because of the risk of:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Lactic acidosis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Especially in:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  AKI   •  Sepsis   •  Severe CKD   •  Hypoxia\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">SGLT2 inhibitors\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These drugs are among the most important advances in CKD management.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examples:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Dapagliflozin   •  Empagliflozin\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Dapagliflozin\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10 mg once daily\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">No titration required.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Benefits\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dapagliflozin:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Reduces proteinuria\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Slows CKD progression\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Decreases hospitalization for HF\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Improves cardiovascular outcomes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Importantly:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These benefits occur even in non-diabetic CKD.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 17\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Genital candidiasis   •  UTI   •  Polyuria   •  Volume depletion   •  Rarely:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Euglycemic DKA\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Caution\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Avoid in:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Severe dehydration   •  Active DKA   •  Type 1 diabetes (unless specialist use)\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. MANAGEMENT OF CKD ANEMIA\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Anemia in CKD occurs primarily because damaged kidneys cannot produce adequate\u003cbr>erythropoietin. Other contributors include iron deficiency, chronic inflammation, blood loss, and\u003cbr>shortened red cell survival.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The typical anemia is:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Normocytic\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Normochromic\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Before treating anemia:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Always assess:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Serum ferritin   •  Transferrin saturation (TSAT)   •  Vitamin B12   •  Folate\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Iron Replacement\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Oral iron\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ferrous sulfate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">200 mg TDS\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 18\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Constipation   •  Black stool   •  Epigastric discomfort\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">IV Iron\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examples:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Iron sucrose   •  Ferric carboxymaltose\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Used if:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Severe deficiency   •  Oral intolerance   •  Dialysis patients\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Erythropoietin (EPO)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examiners love this.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Indication\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Start EPO if:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hb &lt;10 g/dL\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">AFTER correcting:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Iron deficiency   •  Folate deficiency   •  B12 deficiency\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Epoetin alpha\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">50–100 units/kg\u003c/p>\u003ch3 CKD-MINERAL BONE DISEASE (CKD-MBD)\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is one of Nyasatu&#x27;s favorite topics.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">As kidney function declines:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Phosphate excretion decreases.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Serum phosphate rises.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Vitamin D activation decreases.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Calcium absorption falls.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Serum calcium decreases.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Parathyroid hormone rises.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The result is:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Secondary hyperparathyroidism\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">and\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Renal osteodystrophy.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Phosphate Binders\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Calcium Carbonate\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 21\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">500–1500 mg TDS\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Take:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">WITH MEALS\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why with meals?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Because it binds dietary phosphate in the gut before it is absorbed.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is a common viva question.\u003c/p>\u003cp METABOLIC ACIDOSIS\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD patients cannot excrete hydrogen ions adequately.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Result:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Metabolic acidosis.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Treat if:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Serum bicarbonate &lt;22 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 23\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Sodium bicarbonate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">650–1300 mg BD–TDS\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Target:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Serum bicarbonate:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">22–26 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Sodium overload   •  Edema   •  Hypertension\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">7. HYPERKALEMIA\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Very common in CKD.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ECG Changes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Earliest:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Peaked T waves\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Then:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  PR prolongation   •  Wide QRS   •  Sine wave\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Emergency Treatment\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">K ≥6.5 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">OR\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ECG changes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Calcium gluconate\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 24\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10%\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10 mL IV\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Over:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">2–5 minutes.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Protects myocardium.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Insulin + Dextrose\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10 units regular insulin IV\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">25 g dextrose.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Lowers potassium within:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">15–30 min.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Salbutamol nebulization\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10–20 mg\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Sodium bicarbonate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If severe acidosis.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Dialysis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Definitive treatment.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">8. WHEN TO START DIALYSIS?\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is VERY IMPORTANT.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do not use creatinine alone.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">AEIOU\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 25\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">A\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Acidosis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Severe metabolic acidosis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">pH\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">&lt;7.1\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">OR\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Refractory to medical treatment.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">E\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Electrolytes\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Hyperkalemia\u003c/h4>\u003cp
