class=\"note-text-block\">I\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Intoxication\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examples:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Lithium   •  Methanol   •  Ethylene glycol\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">O\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Overload\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Pulmonary edema\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Not responding to diuretics.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">U\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 26\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Uremia\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Symptoms:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Uremic encephalopathy   •  Uremic pericarditis   •  Severe nausea/vomiting   •  Bleeding   •  Severe pruritus\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD Stage 5 and Dialysis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Most patients start dialysis when:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">eGFR\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">&lt;10 mL/min/1.73m²\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">OR\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">eGFR\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">&lt;15 mL/min/1.73m²\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">PLUS\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Symptoms of uremia.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Types of Dialysis\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Hemodialysis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">3 sessions/week.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Each:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Approximately 4 hours.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Peritoneal Dialysis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uses peritoneum as semipermeable membrane.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Transplantation\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Kidney transplantation is the preferred treatment for eligible patients with ESRD because it:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 27\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Improves survival.   •  Improves quality of life.   •  Eliminates dialysis dependence.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">However, patients require lifelong immunosuppression with drugs such as tacrolimus,\u003cbr>mycophenolate mofetil, and corticosteroids.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">EXAMINER FAVORITES\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why calcium carbonate should be taken with meals?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Because it acts as a phosphate binder and binds dietary phosphate inside the gut.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hb is 9 g/dL with normal ferritin. Will you transfuse?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">No.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Give:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Erythropoietin.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why avoid spironolactone in ESRD?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Because:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Severe hyperkalemia.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Target BP in CKD?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">&lt;130/80 mmHg\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Target Hb?\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10–11.5 g/dL\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">eGFR 8 but patient is asymptomatic. Will you dialyze?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Not necessarily.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dialysis is based on:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Symptoms   •  AEIOU indications\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">not eGFR alone.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 28\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why do CKD patients die more from cardiovascular disease than renal failure?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Because CKD accelerates:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Atherosclerosis   •  LVH   •  Heart failure   •  Arrhythmias   •  Vascular calcification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">and cardiovascular disease becomes the leading cause of death in CKD.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CKD COMPLICATION 1:\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">ANEMIA OF CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Anemia is one of the most common complications of chronic kidney disease and becomes\u003cbr>increasingly prevalent as kidney function declines. It usually develops when the glomerular\u003cbr>filtration rate (GFR) falls below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² and is almost universal in patients with end-\u003cbr>stage kidney disease (ESKD). The anemia of CKD is classically described as a normocytic,\u003cbr>normochromic anemia, meaning that the red blood cells are of normal size and color but are\u003cbr>reduced in number. The development of anemia significantly contributes to fatigue, reduced\u003cbr>exercise tolerance, cognitive impairment, left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, and\u003cbr>increased mortality.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF ANEMIA IN CKD\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The primary mechanism responsible for anemia in CKD is reduced erythropoietin (EPO)  production.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Under normal circumstances, the kidneys continuously monitor oxygen delivery to renal tissue.\u003cbr>Specialized fibroblast-like interstitial cells located in the peritubular capillary bed of the renal\u003cbr>cortex produce erythropoietin in response to hypoxia. EPO is then released into the circulation\u003cbr>and acts on the bone marrow to stimulate proliferation and maturation of red blood cell\u003cbr>precursors.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">As CKD progresses, these EPO-producing cells are progressively replaced by fibrotic tissue.\u003cbr>Consequently, the kidney loses its ability to respond appropriately to anemia or hypoxia. Even\u003cbr>when hemoglobin levels fall significantly, the diseased kidney is unable to produce adequate\u003cbr>amounts of EPO. This results in reduced erythropoiesis and chronic anemia.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">However, EPO deficiency is not the only mechanism.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 29\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremic toxins that accumulate in CKD suppress bone marrow function and shorten the lifespan\u003cbr>of circulating red blood cells. Normally, red blood cells survive for approximately 120 days, but\u003cbr>in CKD their lifespan may decrease to 60–90 days. Chronic inflammation also contributes to\u003cbr>anemia through increased production of inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 (IL-6),\u003cbr>which stimulates hepatic synthesis of hepcidin. Hepcidin inhibits intestinal iron absorption and\u003cbr>traps iron within macrophages, producing what is known as functional iron deficiency.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Furthermore, CKD patients often have:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Reduced dietary iron intake\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Gastrointestinal blood loss\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Frequent blood sampling\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Folate deficiency\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Vitamin B12 deficiency\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">All these factors worsen anemia.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">WHY DOES ANEMIA CAUSE HEART FAILURE?\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is a favorite viva question.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Anemia reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood. To compensate, the heart increases\u003cbr>cardiac output by increasing heart rate and stroke volume. Over time, this persistent\u003cbr>hyperdynamic circulation causes left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), ventricular dilatation, and\u003cbr>eventually heart failure.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Therefore:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD → Anemia → Increased cardiac workload → LVH → Heart Failure\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This interaction is part of the:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Cardio-Renal-Anemia Syndrome.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">OTHER CAUSES OF ANEMIA IN CKD\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examiners often ask:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">&quot;Apart from EPO deficiency, what other causes of anemia are there in CKD?&quot;\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mention:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Erythropoietin deficiency (most important)\u003cbr>2. Iron deficiency\u003cbr>3. Chronic inflammation\u003cbr>4. Uremic bone marrow suppression\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 30\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">5. Shortened RBC survival\u003cbr>6. Folate deficiency\u003cbr>7. Vitamin B12 deficiency\u003cbr>8. Gastrointestinal bleeding\u003cbr>9. Hemolysis (less common)\u003cbr>10. Hyperparathyroidism\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CLINICAL FEATURES\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients with anemia of CKD commonly present with:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">General symptoms\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Fatigue   •  Weakness   •  Dizziness   •  Reduced exercise tolerance   •  Palpitations   •  Headache\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Severe anemia\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Dyspnea   •  Angina   •  Heart failure   •  Syncope\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Physical examination\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">You may find:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Pallor   •  Tachycardia   •  Flow murmur   •  Signs of heart failure   •  Koilonychia (if iron deficient)\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">DIAGNOSIS\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The diagnosis of anemia in CKD requires:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Complete Blood Count (CBC)\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Typical findings:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Normocytic\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 31\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">MCV:\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">80–100 fL\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Normochromic\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Normal MCHC.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Example\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hb:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">7.8 g/dL\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">MCV:\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">90 fL\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">MCHC:\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">33%\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This strongly suggests:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Anemia of CKD.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Iron Studies\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Before giving EPO:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ALWAYS evaluate:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Serum ferritin\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">and\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Transferrin saturation (TSAT)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Iron deficiency\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ferritin:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">&lt;100 ng/mL\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">TSAT:\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 32\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">&lt;20%\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Functional iron deficiency\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ferritin:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Normal or elevated\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">TSAT:\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Low\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Occurs because inflammation traps iron within macrophages.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Vitamin B12 and Folate\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Check because:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Vitamin B12 deficiency\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">causes:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Macrocytic anemia.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Folate deficiency\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">also causes:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Macrocytic anemia.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">MANAGEMENT OF ANEMIA OF CKD\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Management begins with identifying and correcting reversible causes.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">A. Iron Replacement\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If iron deficiency is present:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Oral Iron\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Example:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ferrous sulfate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 33\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">200 mg TDS\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effect\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Constipation   •  Black stools   •  Epigastric pain   •  Nausea\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">IV Iron\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examples:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Iron sucrose   •  Ferric carboxymaltose\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Used if:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Dialysis patients   •  Oral intolerance   •  Severe deficiency\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">B. Erythropoietin Therapy (EPO)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is the cornerstone of treatment.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Indications\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Start if:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hb &lt;10 g/dL\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">AFTER correcting:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Iron deficiency   •  Folate deficiency   •  Vitamin B12 deficiency\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Epoetin Alpha\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">50–100 units/kg\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Subcutaneous\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 34\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Three times weekly.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This exact question was asked by:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dr. Akrabi.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Darbepoetin Alpha\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Long acting.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">0.45 mcg/kg weekly\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">or\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Every 2 weeks.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Target Hemoglobin\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do NOT normalize Hb.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Target:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10–11.5 g/dL\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why not target normal Hb?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Because studies showed:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Higher Hb targets increase:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Stroke   •  Hypertension   •  Myocardial infarction   •  Thrombosis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects of EPO\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hypertension   •  Stroke   •  Headache   •  Vascular thrombosis\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">C. BLOOD TRANSFUSION\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 35\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Blood transfusion is NOT first-line therapy.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Indications\u003c/h4>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1.
